clue.text: Delicate walker's for the chop

definitions.meaning: someone who minces walks with small, dainty, affected steps
a kitchen machine for chopping meat finely

explanation.surface: A dainty-stepping person is about to be sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: One who minces walks daintily; the kitchen device of the same name chops meat into small pieces.

clue.text: Unquestioning, I am quietly within the law

parts.note: I'm is the contraction of I am
P is piano, the musical direction for quietly
licit means lawful, permitted by law

explanation.surface: Without question, I am keeping quietly to the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'within' looks like a container signal but belongs to the phrase 'within the law'.
explanation.definitionFit: Implicit faith or trust is absolute, without doubt or question.

clue.text: Mine is the dog on the railway

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the dog sits above the railway

parts.note: a collie is a sheepdog breed
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: The dog on the railway line is mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive but is the coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal pit with its buildings is a mine.

clue.text: Travelling 'salesman at dinner saying his piece again

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative who travels
someone at dinner is eating

explanation.surface: A commercial traveller at the dinner table repeats his patter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone saying his piece again is reciting it once more.

clue.text: Gin? Same again — or just a drop on stage ?

definitions.text: Gin? Same again — or just a drop on stage ?

parts.words: Gin? Same again — or just a drop on stage ?
parts.note: a gin is a snare, and this is another kind of snare, a hinged flap in a theatre floor through which actors drop out of sight

explanation.surface: A drinker orders another gin, or just a small drop, at the theatre bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a bar order, but 'Gin' is the snare for catching animals, 'Same again' says the answer is a snare too, and 'a drop on stage' is the theatrical hatch.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged hatch in a floor is a kind of snare when stepped on, and stage hatches let performers vanish below.

clue.text: Up and around a long time, now he's receiving visitors

definitions.text: Up and around a long time, now he's receiving visitors

parts.words: Up and around a long time, now he's receiving visitors
parts.note: the figure seen in the face of the lunar disc has been up in the sky circling for ages, and astronauts now land there

explanation.surface: An elderly man, long out of bed and active, is now taking callers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up and around' reads as out of a sickbed but means high in the sky, orbiting; the 'visitors' are space travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: The face folklore sees on the lunar surface is the figure up in the night sky, now reached by astronauts.

clue.text: Bravery of reporters holding in a cry of pain

indicators.note: holding in means the word for reporters keeps the cry inside it

parts.note: the press is the body of reporters
ow is what someone cries when hurt

explanation.surface: The courage of journalists who stifle their cries of pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR added 'today!'; the page reads as shown. 'holding in' puts OW inside PRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Prowess is valour or courage, especially in battle.

clue.text: It's high odds against him being one of us

definitions.text: It's high odds against him being one of us

parts.words: It's high odds against him being one of us
parts.note: a racehorse at long odds is unlikely to win, and a stranger is not part of our group

explanation.surface: A remark that he is very unlikely to belong to our circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high odds' is racing talk: the long-priced horse; 'not one of us' is the stranger outside the group.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse given little chance carries long odds, and a person not belonging to the group stands apart.

clue.text: Bird that took a leaf out of the jackdaw's book ?

definitions.text: Bird that took a leaf out of the jackdaw's book ?

parts.words: Bird that took a leaf out of the jackdaw's book ?
parts.note: in the Ingoldsby legend the Jackdaw of Rheims stole the cardinal's ring, and Noah's dove brought back a leaf, so this bird combines both

explanation.surface: A bird that copied the jackdaw's habits.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR garbled the clue; the page reads as shown. 'took a leaf out of his book' means copied him: the Jackdaw of Rheims (an English comic poem) stole a ring, and Noah's dove carried a leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: The wood pigeon has a white neck ring, and the dove is the bird that brought Noah an olive leaf.

clue.text: A bed just like mother used to make ? Hardly

definitions.text: A bed just like mother used to make ? Hardly

parts.words: A bed just like mother used to make ? Hardly
parts.note: the dessert mother bakes is also the name of a prank bed with the sheet folded so legs cannot stretch

explanation.surface: Someone recalls the bed mother used to make, then denies it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just like mother used to make' is the stock phrase for home baking; the bed named after the pudding is a schoolboy prank, which mother would hardly make.
explanation.definitionFit: A prank bed has its sheet folded back so the sleeper's feet stop halfway, named after the homely baked pudding.

clue.text: Where wanderers continue running away ?

parts.note: to bolt is to run away suddenly
to carry on is to go on, so on means continue

explanation.surface: Somewhere aimless travellers keep fleeing.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton Wanderers is an English football club, so its home town is 'Where wanderers' are; the lower case hides the team name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancashire town is home to the football club called the Wanderers.

clue.text: Bird and I have a double bill back at the lake

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
taken as written

indicators.note: back means the doubled bill is read from end to start
double means the abbreviation for bill is written twice over

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A bird and I face two bills on our return to the lakeside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' makes ACAC and 'back' turns it into CACA, which follows TIT and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Titicaca is the large lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia.

clue.text: From where the Duke of Plaza- Toro led his regiment

definitions.text: From where the Duke of Plaza- Toro led his regiment

parts.words: From where the Duke of Plaza- Toro led his regiment
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers the cowardly duke led his regiment from the rear, well away from danger

explanation.surface: A question of where a comic operetta duke commanded his troops.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke of Plaza-Toro, in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Gondoliers, sings that he led his regiment from the rear, in safety.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowardly duke stayed at the rear of his troops, the position at the back.

clue.text: Abuse all round the park

definitions.meaning: railing at someone is scolding or abusing them, so the plural noun means abusive words

explanation.surface: Insults are being hurled everywhere in the park.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranting reproaches are railings; the iron fences that enclose a park share the name.

clue.text: Providing fuel for some grate perhaps

definitions.text: Providing fuel for some grate perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the two words could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Something that supplies fuel for a fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange SOME GRATE; the whole clue then describes the gas holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas holder stores town gas, which fuels gas fires in some hearths.

clue.text: Don't go South to the river

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for South
the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone is told not to head south towards the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tay is Scotland's longest river, flowing out past Dundee.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain where you are is the opposite of leaving.

clue.text: Samson's quickest way to defeat

parts.note: a quicker route is a direct path, and Samson lost his strength when Delilah had his hair cut

explanation.surface: The fastest way to beat the biblical strongman.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson's strength lay in his uncut hair; once it was cropped he was defeated. The phrase also means the most direct route.
explanation.definitionFit: A direct route saves time, and a cropping of hair brought down the biblical strongman.

clue.text: Like the 'deposit everyone put on the high-class bottle ?

indicators.note: put on means the word for everyone is placed before the rest

parts.note: all means everyone
U means upper-class, socially acceptable
a vial is a small glass bottle

explanation.surface: Everyone left a refundable deposit on the posh bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deposit' sounds like a bottle deposit but means silt left by rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Silt and sand laid down by flowing water make a river deposit.

clue.text: Press backing of, for instance, Rugby Union

indicators.note: backing of means the abbreviations for the example and the sport are read from end to start

parts.note: EG, short for exempli gratia, means for instance

explanation.surface: Newspapers are supporting rugby, among other things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing of' turns EGRU round to give the answer; 'Press' looks like the newspapers but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To press someone is to push or encourage them strongly.

clue.text: It's of more than ordinary interest

definitions.text: It's of more than ordinary interest

parts.words: It's of more than ordinary interest
parts.note: interest here is the charge on a loan, and excessive rates are this kind

explanation.surface: Something fascinating beyond the usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interest' looks like fascination but is the money charged on a loan; extortionate rates are the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Lending at excessive rates of interest is moneylending beyond the lawful or normal.

clue.text: Jealousy of Mad Carew at Katmandu

definitions.meaning: in J. Milton Hayes's poem a yellow idol north of Katmandu has the jewel Mad Carew stole

explanation.surface: The envy felt by a reckless man in Nepal.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is the green-eyed monster; the idol's jewel in a famous recitation poem was stolen by Mad Carew.

clue.text: The first person is foremost among them

definitions.text: The first person is foremost among them

parts.words: The first person is foremost among them
parts.note: 'first person' is the grammatical I, and such people put themselves above everyone else

explanation.surface: A remark about who comes first in some group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The first person' is the grammarian's I (Latin ego): self-centred people put I foremost.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-centred people talk constantly about themselves, putting I before all.

clue.text: Openings-in the archipelago, say?

indicators.note: say signals the words should be spoken, matching a word for little islands

parts.note: an archipelago is made up of small islands

explanation.surface: Gaps among the islands, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives a sound-alike: ISLETS, said aloud, gives the small holes for laces.
explanation.definitionFit: Small reinforced holes for laces or cords are openings.

clue.text: Though put to flight the revolutionary holds out

indicators.note: holds means the word for the revolutionary wraps round the word out

parts.note: a red is a communist, a revolutionary
taken as written

explanation.surface: Defeated and chased off, the rebel still refuses to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds out' looks like resisting, but 'holds' puts OUT inside RED.
explanation.definitionFit: An army sent fleeing in disorder has been beaten decisively.

clue.text: Some grow up slippery

parts.note: the slippery elm is a North American species, so some of these tall plants grow up slippery

explanation.surface: Some people become evasive as they grow up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests children turning shifty, but 'slippery' names the slippery elm, a tree species.
explanation.definitionFit: The slippery elm is one species of these tall broadleaved plants.

clue.text: A tool of fraud ?

definitions.meaning: a bladed hand tool for cutting wood or stone
slang for to cheat, so the noun means a swindle

explanation.surface: Asking whether some implement is a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworker's cutting blade; the same word in slang means a swindle or cheat.

clue.text: As passé as the mute dodo, maybe

indicators.note: maybe says the letters of the two words may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Something as out of date as the extinct, silent dodo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' tells you to rearrange MUTE DODO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something passé has gone out of fashion, like the extinct dodo.

clue.text: Scottish charm

parts.note: a lucky charm that is also the title of a novel by the Scottish writer Sir Walter Scott

explanation.surface: The appealing manner of Scots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish' points to Sir Walter Scott, whose novel of the Crusades bears this title; the surface reads it as Scots' charm.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky amulet is a charm, and Walter Scott used the word as the title of a novel.

clue.text: Country lad corrupted ?

parts.note: rus is Latin for the countryside, as in rustic
Ted is a boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A rural boy has been led astray.
explanation.walkthrough: RUS is Latin for country (as in rural and rustic); 'Country lad' reads as one phrase but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal that has oxidised is decayed or eaten away, as rust corrupts iron.
